nameStory: The Transverse Ark gets its name from the distinctive ridges that run across its shell from side to side, rather than from the hinge to the edge like many other clams. The 'ark' part comes from the boat-like shape of these clams when viewed from the side, resembling the curved hull of Noah's ark.
description: The Transverse Ark is a sturdy, medium-sized clam with a distinctive boat-shaped shell marked by prominent ridges running crosswise. These marine mollusks typically grow to about 3-4 inches long and have thick, heavy shells that feel substantial in your hand. Unlike the smooth shells of many clams, Transverse Arks have a rough, textured surface that's easy to recognize. They're filter feeders that burrow partially into sandy or muddy seafloor sediments.

idTips.label: Crosswise ridges
idTips.description: Look for prominent ridges that run perpendicular to the length of the shell, creating a ribbed texture that you can easily feel with your fingertip

idTips.label: Boat-shaped profile
idTips.description: When viewed from the side, the shell has a curved, ark-like shape with a pronounced bulge in the middle

idTips.label: Heavy, thick shell
idTips.description: The shell feels surprisingly heavy for its size and has thick walls that don't break easily when handled

idTips.label: Brownish coloration
idTips.description: Fresh shells are typically brown to grayish-brown on the outside, while beach-worn specimens may fade to whitish or gray

idTips.label: Straight hinge line
idTips.description: The top edge where the shell halves meet is notably straight and long, with numerous small teeth visible when the shell is open

habitat: Look for Transverse Arks in shallow coastal waters along sandy and muddy bottoms, particularly in protected bays and estuaries. In New England, they're most commonly found from the intertidal zone down to about 30 feet deep, often in areas with moderate wave action and good water circulation.

seasonality.spring: Empty shells may wash up on beaches after winter storms, often in good condition due to their sturdy construction.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for finding live specimens in shallow waters during low tides, when they may be partially exposed in the sediment.
seasonality.fall: Shells continue to wash ashore, and this is often the best time for beach collecting as storms become more frequent.
seasonality.winter: Mostly dormant in deeper water, but their heavy shells remain intact and may be found on beaches after storms.

funFact: The Transverse Ark is such a successful traveler that it has invaded the Mediterranean Sea, hitchhiking on ships from North America and establishing thriving populations thousands of miles from home - making it one of the few New England natives that has become an international colonizer!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other ark clams, but the Transverse Ark's crosswise ridges are the key - other ark clams typically have ridges that radiate outward from the hinge like spokes on a wheel. Remember: 'Transverse' means 'across,' so look for ridges that go across the shell.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'ark clams,' these mollusks aren't closely related to the common clams you might eat, like littlenecks or steamers. The ark clam family is actually quite ancient and primitive, with some species dating back hundreds of millions of years in the fossil record.
compareHints: As the only Anadara species in New England waters, the Transverse Ark is most similar to other members of the ark clam family like the Blood Ark. However, it's easily distinguished by its transverse (crosswise) ridges, whereas Blood Arks have radial ridges that fan out from the hinge. The Transverse Ark also tends to be larger and more elongated than most other local ark clams.
